To siphon means to draw liquid out of a container and move it somewhere else through a tube or pipe, usually by creating suction or using gravity to get the flow going. Once the flow starts, the liquid keeps moving on its own.

Picture a simple situation: you need to transfer petrol from a large drum into a smaller container. You put one end of a rubber tube into the drum, the other end into the smaller container (which sits lower down), and you suck on the tube briefly to get the liquid moving. The petrol then flows steadily through the tube and into the new container all by itself — you don't have to keep sucking. That process is called siphoning.

The key physical features of this action are:

  • Liquid is pulled away from a source.
  • It travels through a channel or tube.
  • It ends up somewhere different from where it started.
  • The flow is continuous and steady, not a sudden grab.

In literal, physical contexts, you siphon liquids — petrol, water, chemicals, etc.

"The mechanic siphoned the fuel out of the old tank before replacing it."

"She siphoned water from the large bucket into smaller cups."

"The aquarium owner siphoned the dirty water from the bottom of the tank."

You'll often see it used with out of or from to show the source, and into to show the destination.

"He siphoned petrol out of the truck into a jerry can."
The Figurative Meaning — Where It Gets More Interesting

The word "siphon" has expanded far beyond water and tubes. In everyday language, it's very commonly used figuratively — meaning you apply the same idea (steady, continuous drawing-away) to things like money, resources, talent, attention, or power.

This is where the word really earns its place in the language, because it carries a very specific flavour that other words don't quite match.

When someone says that money is being siphoned, they mean:

  • It is being quietly and steadily drained away from where it belongs.
  • It's going somewhere it was not supposed to go.
  • The process is often gradual — happening little by little over time, not all at once.
  • It is very often done secretly or dishonestly, without the knowledge of the person or institution being drained.

"The finance manager had been siphoning money from the company's accounts for three years before anyone noticed."

"Corrupt officials siphoned billions from public funds that were meant for schools and hospitals."

"The rival company siphoned away our best engineers by offering them higher salaries."

"Social media apps are siphoning attention away from books and deep thinking."

Notice how in every case, there is a source being drained and a destination receiving what flows away. The source loses; the destination gains — often unfairly.

You'll frequently see this as a phrasal verb: to siphon off. This means exactly the same thing, but the word "off" adds a slight emphasis on the idea of separation — the thing being taken is being cut off, removed from where it belongs.

"She siphoned off a portion of the company's profits into her personal account."

"The new school siphoned off students from the older government institutions."

"Energy is being siphoned off from the grid by illegal connections."

Whether you say "siphon" or "siphon off," the meaning is the same. "Siphon off" just sounds slightly more emphatic.
The Nuance That Makes This Word Special

What separates siphon from simpler words like "steal," "take," or "divert" is the combination of three qualities that it always carries:

1. Gradual and ongoing. Siphoning is not a single act of theft — it's a continuous drain. A pickpocket steals your wallet once. Someone who siphons takes a little bit, repeatedly, over a long period. This is why the word feels particularly sinister in financial contexts — it suggests something that has been going on quietly for a long time.

2. Flowing and effortless. Like liquid through a tube, the thing being siphoned moves on its own momentum once the process begins. There's no violent grab — it just quietly flows away. This gives the word a sense of something slipping away almost unnoticed.

3. Redirection from the proper destination. Whatever is being siphoned was supposed to go somewhere specific — a company's profits were meant for shareholders, public funds were meant for citizens, a student's focus was meant for studying. Siphoning means that flow is being quietly hijacked and rerouted.

This is why the word is so useful and so widely used — it captures a specific kind of wrongdoing or loss that no other single word quite describes.

The simplest way to remember it:

To siphon = to steadily draw something away from where it belongs and redirect it elsewhere — often quietly, often dishonestly, and always continuously.

Whether it's petrol being drawn out of a tank, money being quietly drained from an account, or talented people being drawn away from an organisation, the word "siphon" always paints the same picture: a steady, silent, ongoing flow from source to destination — with the source being depleted and usually not knowing (or not being able to stop) what is happening.
